transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Yes, thank you for seeing me. Well, I guess what brings me in is... it's this constant restless feeling I have. It's honestly been driving me a bit crazy lately. I just feel like I’m wound way too tight, all the time, and I can’t fully settle. It's like this physical hum, almost? 

I'm a wholesale buyer, so my days are pretty packed, and even when I’m supposed to be just calmly sitting through a long seasonal planning meeting—which, I mean, those can drag on for hours while we look at spreadsheets and inventory forecasts and argue about shipping delays—I just can't get comfortable. I'm constantly shifting around, feeling that tension. 

But the thing is, it's not just at work when I'm busy. It's everywhere. I try to do things to relax on my weekends, like painting... I started doing these little watercolor landscapes because I read it was supposed to be very mindful and calming, but I can't even sit still for that. Or doing yoga! I go to this yoga studio down the street from my house, and everyone else is resting in child's pose, just totally zen, and I'm on my mat just vibrating, feeling that same tight, coiled-up feeling. My instructor always talks about sinking into the floor and letting go of tension, but I just can't seem to turn it off and settle down, no matter what environment I'm in. I just thought, well, maybe this isn't how everyone else feels all the time, so I finally made an appointment.
Do you ever experience sudden episodes of intense fear or panic, where you feel like something bad is going to happen?

No, no, it's really not like that. I don't get those moments where my heart is pounding because I'm terrified or... or feeling like doom is impending, you know? It's definitely not fear. I know some people get panic attacks—my sister-in-law actually gets them, and she describes it as feeling like the world is ending or she can't breathe, and she has to go sit in a quiet room and do deep breathing just to get through it. 

But for me, it’s completely different. I don't feel like something bad is going to happen at all. If anything, I'm just frustrated because my body just won't cooperate with what I want it to do. Like at the yoga studio I mentioned, I'm not scared of anything, I'm just lying there thinking about the grocery list, and the emails I need to send to our overseas vendors about the spring catalog, and how my foot is itching, and how I desperately need to stretch my legs. It's a physical buzzing, not a scary mental thing. 

So no, no sudden panic or dread. Just this constant... motor running in the background. It's more annoying than scary, honestly. Just really, really annoying when you're trying to review a massive purchase order and you just want to jump out of your chair and pace around the room instead of looking at the screen. But definitely no fear.
Have you noticed that you take less pleasure in things you used to enjoy, or have you felt down or hopeless at times?

Oh, no, definitely not. I mean, I still really love doing things. Like I mentioned the watercolor painting earlier—I really do enjoy the idea of it, and picking out the colors, and looking at the beautiful reference photos of landscapes I want to paint. I actually went down this whole rabbit hole and bought this incredibly nice set of sable brushes online after reading, gosh, probably twenty different art blogs about the best tools for beginners. I have this whole beautiful setup on my dining room table right now. 

It's just that I can't sit there for more than ten minutes without needing to get up and check the mail, or reorganize the spice rack, or walk around the kitchen island. But I still *want* to do it. It's not a lack of interest or a lack of pleasure at all, it's just a lack of... sitting power, I guess? I still get excited about my hobbies and seeing my friends. 

And as for feeling down or hopeless, no, not at all. I mean, sure, I get annoyed or stressed out. Like last week, a massive shipment of spring patio furniture got delayed at the port for three weeks, and I had to deal with all these panicked store managers calling me nonstop. That's just the reality of retail buying, especially lately with all the supply chain headaches we've been having. It can be incredibly stressful, and I'll absolutely vent to my husband about it over dinner, but it doesn't make me feel hopeless about life, you know? It’s just work stress. 

I'm generally a pretty upbeat person. I like my job, I like my life, I love going out to dinner with my friends on Fridays... I just feel like I'm doing all of it with this engine constantly running inside me. So, no, I'm definitely not depressed or losing interest in things, just... constantly revving. I just wish I could sit still long enough to actually finish one of those paintings!
Do you find it difficult to focus or stay attentive, especially during tasks that require sustained mental effort?

Well, no, not really. I don't think it's a focus issue, honestly. I mean, sure, those seasonal planning meetings I mentioned? They can be incredibly dry. We'll be looking at, you know, Q3 projections for patio umbrellas, and the spreadsheet will have a hundred rows, and the lighting in the conference room is always that terrible fluorescent kind that gives you a headache if you look at it too long. And yes, my mind will wander a bit during those, but I feel like that's just human nature, right? Who wouldn't zone out a little when someone is droning on about freight costs for an hour? 

But when it comes down to actual mental effort, like when I really need to get something done? I can focus just fine. If I have a deadline to finalize a purchase order for a new vendor, or if I'm negotiating pricing and I really have to pay attention to the margins, I am locked in. I don't lose my train of thought or forget what I'm doing. I just... I might be bouncing my leg under the desk the entire time, or I might need to stand up and pace around my office while I'm on the phone with the supplier, but my brain is fully engaged in the task. 

It's the physical part of sitting still that gets me, not the mental part of focusing. Like, I can read a whole contract and understand every word, I just can't do it while sitting perfectly still in a chair. I usually end up taking my laptop to the kitchen counter so I can stand, or I'll read it on my tablet while walking on the treadmill. So, no, I wouldn't say I have trouble staying attentive. My brain works just fine, it's just my body that won't stop moving while my brain is working.
Do you ever notice physical symptoms like muscle tension, restlessness, or an increased heart rate even when you're not in a stressful situation or actively thinking about something worrying?

Well, I definitely feel restless, but I wouldn't call it muscle tension or an increased heart rate, and it's certainly not tied to worrying. Like I was saying before, it's just this constant physical need to move. It's not like my muscles are tight because I'm stressed, it's more like they're... energized? I don't know if that's the right word. 

For example, last Sunday, we had absolutely nothing going on. No plans, no errands, nothing. My husband was perfectly content to just sit in his recliner and watch a three-hour documentary about the history of the postal service—which, bless him, he found fascinating, but I just couldn't do it. I wasn't worried about anything, work was fine, the house was clean, but I just couldn't sit there on the couch with him. My legs just felt like they needed to be doing something. So I ended up reorganizing the entire linen closet. I pulled everything out, refolded all the towels so the edges were perfectly aligned, sorted the sheets by size and season... I even found this old set of flannel sheets we bought for a ski trip to Vermont like eight years ago that we haven't used since. 

And the whole time I was doing it, my heart wasn't racing, I wasn't tense, I was actually having a pretty good time! It just felt good to be moving around and doing something with my hands. So, yes to the restlessness, absolutely, but it's not a nervous restlessness. It's just... I guess my default state is "in motion." Even when I'm relaxed, my version of relaxed is just doing a low-stakes activity instead of a high-stakes one. Sitting perfectly still just isn't in my repertoire, whether I'm stressed or not.

Do you notice this restlessness even in situations where you're completely alone and there's no external pressure or expectation to be doing something, like when you're trying to fall asleep or just sitting quietly with nothing to do?

Oh, absolutely. It doesn't matter if I'm alone, if I'm with people, if I'm at work, or if I'm at home. That's actually the main reason I'm here, to be honest. It's this constant restless feeling. It's like... like I'm wound too tight, you know? And I just can't fully settle down. 

Even when I'm supposed to be doing something relaxing! Like, I tried yoga. A few of my friends go to this studio downtown, and they absolutely swear by it for stress relief and centering yourself, or whatever. So I went with them, and it was a lovely studio, smelled like lavender, soft music playing... but I was miserable. The whole time, the instructor is telling us to hold these poses and breathe, and I'm just lying there on the mat, staring at the ceiling, thinking, "Okay, how much longer? Can we move to the next thing? My foot is twitching. I need to stretch my arm." I just couldn't settle into it. 

And it's the same thing with the watercolor painting I mentioned earlier, or even just sitting through one of those planning meetings at work. It doesn't matter if it's a hobby I want to do, or a meeting I have to do, or trying to fall asleep at night. I'll get into bed, the room is dark, my husband is snoring softly next to me, and my brain is quiet, but my body is just... buzzing. I'll toss and turn, I'll readjust the blankets, I'll stick one foot out, then pull it back in. It's just this inescapable feeling that I need to be in motion, even when there is absolutely nothing I need to be doing.
Have you ever felt an inner urge to move that you couldn't control, even when you wanted to stay still, like a feeling of inner restlessness that wasn't about being anxious or stressed?

Yes, exactly! That is exactly what I was just trying to say. That specific feeling is actually what brings me in here to see you. It’s this constant restless feeling, and you hit the nail on the head—it has absolutely nothing to do with being anxious or stressed. I’m not sitting there worrying about my purchase orders or whether the freight shipments from overseas are going to clear customs on time. 

It’s just... like I said, it’s like I’m wound too tight. You know those little wind-up toys where you turn the key in the back one too many times and it just vibrates because it has to release that energy? That’s what it feels like inside. I just can’t fully settle, even when I want to. And it’s so frustrating because it happens right when I’m supposed to be calmly sitting there! 

Like I mentioned with those seasonal planning meetings—I want to just sit in the conference chair like everyone else and politely listen to the Q3 projections, but I have this uncontrollable inner urge to shift, to tap my pen, to stand up and walk to the back of the room. Or with the watercolor painting I tried to get into, or that disastrous yoga class with my friends. You’d think with watercolors, you’re just sitting there peacefully making pretty strokes on the paper, letting the colors bleed into each other, but my inner motor is just humming the entire time. I want to stay still, I really do, especially when I’m trying to do something relaxing or when it’s socially expected of me to just sit quietly, but that inner restlessness just overrides whatever my brain is trying to tell my body to do.
When did you first start noticing this restless feeling? Was it something you remember feeling even as a child, or did it start more recently in adulthood?

Oh, it's definitely not a recent thing. Not at all. I mean, I've been like this for as long as I can remember, honestly. It's funny you ask about childhood, because it really takes me back. I was always the kid who just... couldn't stay put. 

I distinctly remember being in elementary school—second grade, I think, Mrs. Gable's class. She had this big, colorful rug where we were all supposed to sit cross-legged for story time or morning announcements or whatever. And I just couldn't do it. I mean, I'd start out fine, but within two minutes, my legs would start aching to move, and I'd be shifting around, and then before I knew it, I was popping up out of my seat. I wasn't trying to be bad or disruptive, I just physically could not stay glued to that rug. 

And my poor parents, they were always getting notes sent home. "She won't stay in her seat," "She's constantly interrupting," that kind of thing. Because that was the other part of it—it wasn't just the physical movement, it was like my mouth was restless, too. If the teacher was asking a question, I'd be blurting out the answer before she even finished her sentence. I just had this overwhelming urge to jump in, to get it out, to keep things moving. I'd talk over my classmates, too, not because I didn't care what they had to say, but because waiting my turn felt like physical torture. It's like that wind-up toy feeling I was talking about earlier—if I couldn't move my body, the energy would just come out of my mouth instead. 

So, yes, it's been there forever. It's not something that just cropped up when I started working as a buyer or when life got more complicated. It's just... me. It's how I've always been wired, right back to the days of Mrs. Gable's story time rug.
As a child, did you have trouble staying focused on tasks or organizing your work, even when you were trying to pay attention?

No, actually. That's the funny thing about it. Everyone always assumes that if you're bouncing off the walls, your brain must be bouncing all over the place too, but that really wasn't the case for me. I didn't have any trouble focusing on my schoolwork or organizing my things. 

In fact, I was a pretty good student when it came to the actual work. I remember in fourth grade, Mr. Henderson's class—he had this incredibly strict system for our desks. We had these little plastic bins inside, and the math workbook had to be on the left, the spelling journal on the right, and all our pencils had to be sharpened and facing the same way in the pencil case. Most of the kids hated it, but I actually loved it. I kept my desk immaculate. I never lost my homework, I always knew exactly where my assignments were, and I could sit down and power through a worksheet without getting distracted by what was happening outside the window or what the kid next to me was doing. 

My problem was never about paying attention to the task itself. If I had a math test in front of me, I was laser-focused on those fractions. I'd finish it in record time, actually. But that was the issue—once I was done, or if the teacher was just talking and I didn't have something active to do with my hands or my brain, that's when the restlessness would kick in. I'd finish my spelling test and immediately start tapping my pencil, or kicking the leg of my chair, or trying to talk to my best friend, Sarah, who sat two rows over. 

So the organization and the focus? Totally fine. I was never the kid who forgot her backpack on the bus or couldn't finish a reading assignment because she kept losing her place. It was strictly that physical need to move, that inability to just exist quietly in a space once the actual work was done. Even now, as a buyer, my spreadsheets are color-coded and my purchase orders are meticulously organized. I can focus on the numbers all day long. I just can't sit still while I'm doing it.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about an inner urge to move and inner restlessness, which directly maps to the adult manifestation of this symptom (feeling restless).

patient.answer:
Yes, exactly! That is exactly what I was just trying to say. That specific feeling is actually what brings me in here to see you. It’s this constant restless feeling, and you hit the nail on the head—it has absolutely nothing to do with being anxious or stressed. I’m not sitting there worrying about my purchase orders or whether the freight shipments from overseas are going to clear customs on time. 

It’s just... like I said, it’s like I’m wound too tight. You know those little wind-up toys where you turn the key in the back one too many times and it just vibrates because it has to release that energy? That’s what it feels like inside. I just can’t fully settle, even when I want to. And it’s so frustrating because it happens right when I’m supposed to be calmly sitting there! 

Like I mentioned with those seasonal planning meetings—I want to just sit in the conference chair like everyone else and politely listen to the Q3 projections, but I have this uncontrollable inner urge to shift, to tap my pen, to stand up and walk to the back of the room. Or with the watercolor painting I tried to get into, or that disastrous yoga class with my friends. You’d think with watercolors, you’re just sitting there peacefully making pretty strokes on the paper, letting the colors bleed into each other, but my inner motor is just humming the entire time. I want to stay still, I really do, especially when I’m trying to do something relaxing or when it’s socially expected of me to just sit quietly, but that inner restlessness just overrides whatever my brain is trying to tell my body to do.

doctor.intent: Determine if symptoms are present from childhood, a key criterion for ADHD, which differentiates it from other anxiety or restlessness-related disorders.
doctor.question: When did you first start noticing this restless feeling? Was it something you remember feeling even as a child, or did it start more recently in adulthood?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: I remember in elementary school getting notes sent home because I kept popping out of my seat, talking over classmates, and rushing to answer before the teacher finished the question.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about when the restless feeling first started, specifically inquiring if it was present during childhood, which aligns with the onset prior to age 12 years criterion.

patient.answer:
Oh, it's definitely not a recent thing. Not at all. I mean, I've been like this for as long as I can remember, honestly. It's funny you ask about childhood, because it really takes me back. I was always the kid who just... couldn't stay put. 

I distinctly remember being in elementary school—second grade, I think, Mrs. Gable's class. She had this big, colorful rug where we were all supposed to sit cross-legged for story time or morning announcements or whatever. And I just couldn't do it. I mean, I'd start out fine, but within two minutes, my legs would start aching to move, and I'd be shifting around, and then before I knew it, I was popping up out of my seat. I wasn't trying to be bad or disruptive, I just physically could not stay glued to that rug. 

And my poor parents, they were always getting notes sent home. "She won't stay in her seat," "She's constantly interrupting," that kind of thing. Because that was the other part of it—it wasn't just the physical movement, it was like my mouth was restless, too. If the teacher was asking a question, I'd be blurting out the answer before she even finished her sentence. I just had this overwhelming urge to jump in, to get it out, to keep things moving. I'd talk over my classmates, too, not because I didn't care what they had to say, but because waiting my turn felt like physical torture. It's like that wind-up toy feeling I was talking about earlier—if I couldn't move my body, the energy would just come out of my mouth instead. 

So, yes, it's been there forever. It's not something that just cropped up when I started working as a buyer or when life got more complicated. It's just... me. It's how I've always been wired, right back to the days of Mrs. Gable's story time rug.

inference.note: This turn added F90.0 (Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, predominantly inattentive type) as a candidate due to the patient's lifelong history of restlessness, difficulty remaining seated, and inner motoric agitation, consistent with ADHD symptoms. The restlessness described is not tied to anxiety, depression, or trauma, but rather a chronic, persistent inner urge to move, dating back to childhood. Other candidates remain due to overlapping symptoms of anxiety (F40.00, F41.1, F41.9), stress-related disorders (F43.20, F43.21, F43.22, F43.23), dissociative disorders (F44.8), and mood disorders (F48.0, F48.1), which have not yet been ruled out.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of inattention or disorganization that could support a diagnosis of ADHD, especially since hyperactivity and restlessness are already endorsed.
doctor.question: As a child, did you have trouble staying focused on tasks or organizing your work, even when you were trying to pay attention?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about childhood symptoms of inattention and disorganization. My symptom profile does not include information about childhood inattention or organization; my childhood symptoms (Additional Requirement 1) only mention hyperactivity and impulsivity.

patient.answer:
No, actually. That's the funny thing about it. Everyone always assumes that if you're bouncing off the walls, your brain must be bouncing all over the place too, but that really wasn't the case for me. I didn't have any trouble focusing on my schoolwork or organizing my things. 

In fact, I was a pretty good student when it came to the actual work. I remember in fourth grade, Mr. Henderson's class—he had this incredibly strict system for our desks. We had these little plastic bins inside, and the math workbook had to be on the left, the spelling journal on the right, and all our pencils had to be sharpened and facing the same way in the pencil case. Most of the kids hated it, but I actually loved it. I kept my desk immaculate. I never lost my homework, I always knew exactly where my assignments were, and I could sit down and power through a worksheet without getting distracted by what was happening outside the window or what the kid next to me was doing. 

My problem was never about paying attention to the task itself. If I had a math test in front of me, I was laser-focused on those fractions. I'd finish it in record time, actually. But that was the issue—once I was done, or if the teacher was just talking and I didn't have something active to do with my hands or my brain, that's when the restlessness would kick in. I'd finish my spelling test and immediately start tapping my pencil, or kicking the leg of my chair, or trying to talk to my best friend, Sarah, who sat two rows over. 

So the organization and the focus? Totally fine. I was never the kid who forgot her backpack on the bus or couldn't finish a reading assignment because she kept losing her place. It was strictly that physical need to move, that inability to just exist quietly in a space once the actual work was done. Even now, as a buyer, my spreadsheets are color-coded and my purchase orders are meticulously organized. I can focus on the numbers all day long. I just can't sit still while I'm doing it.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms of persistent physical restlessness, inability to remain still, and a constant inner urge to move, present since childhood, strongly suggest ADHD, predominantly hyperactive/impulsive presentation. Other anxiety disorders (F40.00, F41.1, F41.9), adjustment disorders (F43.20, F43.21, F43.22, F43.23), dissociative disorders (F44.8), and mood disorders (F48.0, F48.1) have been ruled out based on the absence of anxiety, panic, depressive symptoms, or stressor-linked onset. No evidence of inattention was reported, supporting the diagnosis of F90.0 over other subtypes of ADHD.
